projects.title: Sign Finder
projects.summary: An iOS app that identifies UK road signs from a photo or the live camera, built as my final year project. Everything runs on the device, so no image ever leaves the phone. In good conditions the model reached up to 96% accuracy.
features: Scan a road sign from a photo, with bounding boxes and confidence scores
Live camera scan that overlays boxes on the moving feed
Road sign information screen, grouped by sign type, for revision
Settings for camera quality and how often frames are analysed, to save battery
Fully offline and private: images are never stored or uploaded
Custom dataset merged from public sets plus my own annotated photos
projects.whatILearned:
The problem: signs are easy to miss or misread, especially for learner drivers and tourists, and built-in sign recognition only exists in newer, expensive cars. I wanted a free tool that works on any iPhone, both as a quick "what does that sign mean?" helper and as a revision aid for the driving test.

The dataset: public datasets used different layouts (Pascal VOC XML, CSV) and some contained duplicate boxes or signs that do not exist in the UK. I wrote Python scripts to convert everything into one format, drop duplicates and filter out irrelevant classes, then added my own photos annotated by hand in LabelImg. Only datasets with reuse licences were used and they are credited in the report.

The models: I first trained a TensorFlow object detector, which scored above 90%, but converting it to Core ML with coremltools made accuracy drop badly. After researching lightweight options (SSD-MobileNet, YOLOv5 Nano, EfficientDet) I switched to Create ML, whose YOLOv2-style detector drops straight into Xcode, and that gave the reliable result I needed. Lesson learned: check the deployment path before committing to a training framework.

The app: SwiftUI for the screens, Vision and Core ML for inference, AVFoundation for the camera. The Scan button stays disabled until a photo is chosen, and the live camera never starts on launch, which came out of black-box testing.

Limitations and future work: the model struggles with signs that are far away, at odd angles or in poor light, and rarer signs such as no-entry were sometimes mistaken for common ones like speed limits because the public data was unbalanced. A broader, more balanced set of photos taken in varied conditions is the clear next step, followed by more languages and theme options. The full report is summarised here rather than published.

story.label: Problem
story.title: Why this app exists
body: Road signs are easy to miss or misread, especially for learner drivers and visitors, and built-in sign recognition only exists in newer, expensive cars. I wanted a free tool that works on any iPhone, both as a quick "what does that sign mean?" helper and as a revision aid for the driving test.

That gave me three design rules that shaped everything else: it has to work from a single photo, it has to work live through the camera, and it has to be private, so every image is processed on the phone and never stored or uploaded.

story.label: Data
story.title: Building the dataset
body: Public datasets used different layouts (Pascal VOC XML, CSV), some had duplicate boxes, and some contained signs that do not exist in the UK. I wrote Python scripts to convert everything into one format, drop duplicates and filter out irrelevant classes, then added my own photos annotated by hand in LabelImg. Only datasets with reuse licences were used.
The first job of every script is the same: read an annotation file and return the image plus a list of labelled boxes.

notes.title: Why Pascal VOC as the common format?
notes.text: LabelImg saves in Pascal VOC, so my own photos already matched it. Converting the other datasets into the same shape meant the rest of the pipeline only ever had to understand one format.

notes.title: Why return the filename and a list of tuples?
notes.text: Each image can hold several signs, so an image maps to a list of (label, box) pairs. Keeping the label and the four corner coordinates together made it easy to build the label list and the multi-sign training matrix afterwards.

notes.title: Why read the filename from the XML?
notes.text: The annotation is the source of truth for which image it describes, so pairing the two never depends on files being sorted the same way in two folders.

story.label: Model
story.title: Choosing a model that can ship
body: I first trained a TensorFlow convolutional network: three convolution and pooling stages (32, 64 and 128 filters), a dropout layer to reduce overfitting and a sigmoid output so one image can contain several signs. It scored above 90%, but converting it to Core ML with coremltools made the accuracy drop badly.

After researching lightweight options (SSD-MobileNet, YOLOv5 Nano, EfficientDet) I switched to Create ML, whose YOLOv2-style detector drops straight into Xcode. The lesson was to check the deployment path before committing to a training framework. The final model reached up to 96% accuracy in good conditions.

story.label: Photo scan
story.title: Photo scan: boxes in the right place
body: The scan screen lets you pick a photo, runs the model through Vision, and draws a labelled box over every sign it finds with the confidence score underneath. The Scan button stays disabled until a photo is chosen, which came out of black-box testing: pressing it with nothing selected used to be a dead end.

notes.title: Why a GeometryReader?
notes.text: Vision returns each box as fractions of the image (0 to 1). The image is shown at whatever size fits, so I read the real width and height from the GeometryReader and multiply, which keeps the boxes on the signs on any screen.

notes.title: Why 1 minus y minus height?
notes.text: Vision measures from the bottom-left corner but SwiftUI measures from the top-left. Flipping the y value is what stops the boxes appearing upside down.

notes.title: Why a ZStack?
notes.text: The image, the box outline and the label need to sit on top of one another at exact positions, so each box and its label are positioned inside the same ZStack as the picture.

notes.title: Why a guard on the image conversion?
notes.text: Converting between UIImage and CGImage can fail, and a guard turns that into a readable message instead of a crash.

story.label: Live scan
story.title: Live scan without draining the battery
body: The live tab reads frames from the camera and overlays boxes on the moving feed. Running a neural network on all 30 or more frames a second would heat the phone and drain the battery, so the design is about doing less work: analyse every Nth frame, keep the heavy work off the main thread, and only start the camera when the user presses start.

notes.title: Why every Nth frame?
notes.text: A counter and a modulo check let the app skip most frames. The interval is a setting, so a user can trade smoothness for battery life.

notes.title: Why a separate queue for the model?
notes.text: Inference is slow compared with drawing. Running it on its own background queue keeps the camera preview and the buttons responsive, and results are sent back to the main thread only to update the boxes.

notes.title: Why [weak self]?
notes.text: The Vision callback can fire after the screen has gone. A weak reference stops the callback from keeping the view model alive after the user leaves.

notes.title: Why scaleFill?
notes.text: The model expects a fixed input size, so each frame is scaled to fill it rather than cropped, which keeps signs near the edges in view.

story.label: Info and settings
story.title: Revision screen and settings
body: A recognised sign is only useful if you know what it means, so the info tab lists signs grouped by type for revision. The settings screen exposes the two choices that matter most on a phone: camera quality and how often frames are analysed. Both feed straight into the live scan, so a user on an older phone can lower them.

projects.title: Sudoku Solver
projects.summary: A Sudoku solver that deduces as much as it can with logic and only guesses when it has to. It solves the hardest puzzles in about 5 ms, and follows the approach from Peter Norvig's essay on solving every Sudoku puzzle.
features: Every square tracks the digits still possible there
Two rules cascade: a single-candidate square removes that digit from its 20 peers, and a digit with only one home in a row, column or box is placed
Backtracking search only when logic stalls, guessing in the square with the fewest candidates
Small desktop app with a one-click launcher
Unit tests check every row, column and box holds 1 to 9 exactly once
Timing: easy ~7 ms, hardest known puzzle ~5 ms, 17-clue puzzle ~4 ms
projects.whatILearned:
Brute force would try 9^81 combinations, more than the atoms in the universe, so the interesting part is cutting the search space. Each square starts as "any of 1 to 9". Two rules then fire repeatedly: if a square is down to one digit, no peer can use it; if a digit fits in only one square of a row, column or box, it goes there. These rules cascade, so an easy puzzle collapses with no guessing at all.

When logic stalls, the solver guesses in the square with the fewest options (a two-option guess is right half the time), propagates the consequences, and backs out if it hits a contradiction.

Results: the easy puzzle is fully solved by logic alone, the "hardest ever" puzzle has 33 of 81 squares solved by logic before the search starts, and the 17-clue puzzle (the proven minimum) needs no guessing. The main limitation is that each guess copies the whole board; real solvers undo moves instead. Ideas for next time: a puzzle generator with unique solutions, a difficulty rating based on how far logic gets, and reading a puzzle from a photo with OCR.

story.label: Idea
story.title: Cut the search space, do not brute force it
body: Brute force would try 9 to the power of 81 combinations, more than the atoms in the universe, so the interesting part is cutting the search space. I followed the approach from Peter Norvig's essay: let logic do as much work as possible and only guess when logic stalls.

story.label: Board
story.title: Representing the board
body: Squares are named A1 to I9. Every row, column and 3x3 box is a unit, giving 27 units of 9 squares, and each square has exactly 20 peers that share a unit with it. These are built once, up front, so the solving code never has to work out neighbours again.
Each square stores a string of the digits still possible there. An empty square starts as 123456789 and a solved one is a single digit, so the same structure holds both the clues and the working.

story.label: Logic
story.title: Eliminate: two rules that cascade
body: Eliminating a digit from a square can trigger two consequences. If a square is down to one digit, no peer can use it. If a digit only fits in one square of a row, column or box, it must go there. Each rule can trigger the other, so an easy puzzle collapses with no guessing at all.

notes.title: Why store candidates as a string?
notes.text: Removing a digit is one replace call and the length tells me how many options remain. A string is also easy to print for debugging.

notes.title: Why return False on an empty square?
notes.text: A square with no candidates is a contradiction. Returning False up the chain tells the search that its last guess was wrong, so it can back out.

notes.title: Why recursion?
notes.text: Each elimination can cause further eliminations. Recursion lets the consequences ripple through the board until nothing changes, with no need for a separate loop.

notes.title: Why check each unit for one place left?
notes.text: This is the rule people use by hand: if only one square in a row can hold a 7, it must be a 7. Without it, the solver would need many more guesses.

story.label: Search
story.title: Search only when logic stalls
body: When logic runs out, the solver guesses. It picks the unsolved square with the fewest options, because a two-option guess is right half the time, tries each digit on a copy of the board, propagates the consequences and backs out if it hits a contradiction.

notes.title: Why the fewest candidates first?
notes.text: A square with two options halves the work immediately, while a square with nine would barely cut anything. Fewest-first keeps the search tree narrow.

notes.title: Why copy the values?
notes.text: Each guess changes the board. Working on a copy means a wrong guess can be thrown away without having to undo any moves, at the cost of copying the board each time.

notes.title: Why does it return the first success?
notes.text: Valid Sudoku puzzles have one solution, so as soon as one branch reaches a full board the search can stop.

story.label: Testing
story.title: Proving it is correct and fast
body: The tests check the structure first (81 squares, 27 units, 20 peers each), then solve an easy puzzle, the hardest known puzzle and the 17-clue minimum puzzle, and verify that every row, column and box holds 1 to 9 exactly once. Timings are printed too: roughly 7 ms for easy, 5 ms for the hardest and 4 ms for the 17-clue puzzle, and the test also reports how many squares propagation alone filled before any guessing.

story.label: App
story.title: A small desktop app on top
body: A Tkinter window gives a 9x9 grid of entry boxes with thicker borders around each box, key-by-key validation so only digits are accepted, and a one-click launcher. Before solving, the app checks the clues for duplicates so it can tell the difference between invalid input and a puzzle with no solution, and says which row, column or box is wrong.

projects.title: Theatre Booking System (C++)
projects.summary: A console theatre booking app written in C++, rebuilt from my 2022 Java coursework to practise object-oriented design and unit testing in a different language.
features: Menu to buy a ticket, cancel a ticket and list available seats
Seat map printed row by row, with booked seats marked
Save seating to a file and load it back
Print ticket information and total price, and sort tickets by price
Input validation for rows, seats and menu choices
Catch unit tests covering seats, rows, the auditorium, tickets and people
projects.whatILearned:
Class design: Ticket holds the row, seat and price; Person holds the customer details; Row owns the state of each seat (free or booked, using an enum class); Auditorium owns the rows and their prices. Booking and cancelling go through Row so the rules live in one place, and the menu code in Main only talks to those classes.

Testing: nine Catch test cases check that a new row starts free, booking a free seat works, double-booking fails, cancelling frees the seat, out-of-range seats are rejected, the auditorium is built with the expected rows and prices, and that tickets and people return the values they were created with.

The project began as the Java version (see the early work section). Porting it showed me what changes between languages: manual header files, const correctness, value versus reference semantics and no garbage collector, while the design carried over almost unchanged.

story.label: Design
story.title: Four classes, each with one job
body: The project started as a Java coursework and I rebuilt it in C++ to practise object-oriented design and unit testing in a different language. Ticket holds the row, seat and price and a Person; Person holds the customer details; Row owns the state of each seat; Auditorium owns the rows and their prices.
The menu code in Main only talks to those classes, so the booking rules live in one place.

story.label: Rules
story.title: Row owns the booking rules
body: Booking and cancelling go through Row. A seat is either free or booked, and nothing outside Row can put a seat into a state the rules do not allow.

notes.title: Why an enum class for seat state?
notes.text: SeatState has two values, Free and Booked. An enum class cannot be mixed up with an int or another enum, so a seat can never hold an invalid state.

notes.title: Why does isFree check the range?
notes.text: The bounds check and the state check sit in one function, so out-of-range seats are simply never free and book() cannot touch memory outside the vector.

notes.title: Why does book return a bool?
notes.text: The caller needs to know whether it worked so the menu can say seat taken instead of printing a ticket for a seat that was already booked.

notes.title: Why seat minus one?
notes.text: People count seats from 1 but the vector counts from 0. Converting in one place inside Row keeps the rest of the program in human numbering.

story.label: Layout
story.title: Auditorium, tickets and the menu
body: The auditorium is built with three rows of 12, 16 and 20 seats priced at 3, 6 and 9 pounds. The menu lets you buy a ticket, cancel one, print the seat map row by row with booked seats marked, list tickets with the total price, sort them by price, and save the seating to a file and load it back. Every input is validated for row, seat and menu choice.

story.label: Testing
story.title: Tests written as sentences
body: Nine Catch test cases cover rows, the auditorium, tickets and people. Each test name reads as a sentence about behaviour, so the test output doubles as a specification.

notes.title: Why test names as sentences?
notes.text: When one fails, the name says what rule broke, such as booking an already booked seat fails, without opening the code.

notes.title: Why does every test build its own Row?
notes.text: Tests that share no state cannot affect each other, so they pass or fail for one reason and can run in any order.

notes.title: Why test the failure case?
notes.text: Double booking is the bug that matters most in a booking system, so there is a test that tries to book the same seat twice and expects it to be refused.

projects.title: iOS Weather App
projects.summary: A SwiftUI weather app with current conditions, hourly and daily forecasts, air quality, a map of tourist attractions and a list of saved places. Built for a mobile development module, with two extra features of my own.
features: Current weather for the selected city, with air quality
Hourly and daily forecast screens
Map of tourist attractions around the chosen place
Visited places list with swipe actions
My enhancement: tap an attraction to recentre the map on it
My enhancement: swipe right on a saved place to refresh its weather
projects.whatILearned:
The app is split into views (current, hourly, daily, forecast, map, visited places and a tab bar) and view models that fetch and decode data from the OpenWeatherMap forecast and air pollution services. Keeping networking out of the views made each screen small and easy to change.

My two enhancements aimed at everyday friction. Tapping an attraction in the list recentres the map on it, which helps when attractions are close together or hard to find. Swiping right on a saved place shows a button that pulls fresh data for that city, mirroring the familiar swipe-left-to-delete gesture.

I learned SwiftUI state and navigation, MapKit annotations, decoding JSON into Swift models, and handling asynchronous loading so screens do not show stale data.

story.label: Structure
story.title: Views, view models and models
body: The app is split into views (current, hourly, daily, forecast, map, visited places and a tab bar), a view model that fetches and prepares the data, and model structs that match the JSON from the weather services. Keeping networking out of the views made each screen small and easy to change.

story.label: Data
story.title: From a city name to a forecast
body: Typing a city triggers a chain: the city is geocoded into coordinates, those coordinates are used to request the forecast and the air quality from OpenWeatherMap, the JSON is decoded into Swift models, and finally nearby tourist attractions are searched for. Each step is async and the HTTP status is checked before decoding, so a failed request does not show stale or broken data. Results are published back on the main thread so SwiftUI updates the screens.

story.label: Map
story.title: A map that helps you find attractions
body: The map shows the five top tourist attractions around the chosen place, found with a local map search over a small region. Under the map is a list of the same places. My first enhancement makes the list useful: tap an attraction and the map recentres on it, which helps when attractions are close together or hard to spot.

notes.title: Why is the map region state?
notes.text: The map is bound to a region value. Changing the region's centre in the tap handler is all that is needed for SwiftUI to move the map.

notes.title: Why change only the centre?
notes.text: Keeping the zoom as it was means the map pans to the place rather than jumping to a different scale, which feels more natural.

notes.title: Why attach the tap to each row?
notes.text: The whole row is the tap target, not just the pin, which is easier to hit on a phone.

story.label: Saved places
story.title: Visited places and a swipe to reload
body: Saved places are stored with SwiftData and shown in a list. Swiping left deletes a place, which is the gesture people already know. My second enhancement adds the opposite swipe: swiping right on a saved place loads its weather again, so the other tabs update without typing the city name.

notes.title: Why the leading edge?
notes.text: Trailing swipes are for destructive actions like delete. Putting the safe action on the opposite side stops people deleting a place by accident.

notes.title: Why a Task?
notes.text: Loading the place is async. A Task lets the button call await code without blocking the interface.

notes.title: Why set the city on the view model?
notes.text: The view model is shared by every tab, so setting the city and reloading updates the current, hourly, daily and map screens together.

projects.title: Applied AI: RNN Sentiment Analysis
projects.summary: A simple recurrent neural network that classifies tweets as positive or negative, reaching 85.3% test accuracy, with a written comparison of CNN and RNN approaches to text and speech recognition.
features: Data pipeline: load only the label and text columns, map labels to 0 and 1, tokenise to a 10,000 word vocabulary and pad to 100 tokens
Model: embedding layer, 32-unit simple RNN and a sigmoid output
85.3% test accuracy (loss 0.348) on a 70/30 train and test split
Confusion matrix showing where the model goes wrong
Prediction function that cleans and classifies any new sentence
projects.whatILearned:
The data is a public tweet sentiment set labelled negative or positive. Cleaning it meant keeping the two useful columns, converting the labels to 0 and 1, turning words into integer tokens and padding every tweet to the same length so the network can process them in batches.

The model is deliberately small: an embedding layer that learns a vector per word, one simple RNN layer that reads the tweet in order, and a single sigmoid neuron for the probability of positive. It trained for five epochs and scored 85.3% on unseen tweets.

The confusion matrix showed a bias toward predicting negative, because the data I could download was imbalanced. Balancing by throwing away data would have cost more accuracy than it fixed. Natural improvements are an LSTM, which copes better with vanishing gradients, and a longer vocabulary and sequence length so long tweets do not lose words.

story.label: Data
story.title: A tweet sentiment dataset
body: The data is a public tweet sentiment set labelled negative or positive. Cleaning it meant keeping only the two useful columns (the label and the text), reading the file with the right encoding, and turning the labels into 0 and 1.

story.label: Text to numbers
story.title: Turning words into numbers
body: A network cannot read words, so each tweet becomes a list of integers. A tokenizer keeps the 10,000 most common words and maps anything else to an out-of-vocabulary token, then every tweet is padded to 100 tokens so they can be processed in batches. The data was split 70/30 into training and test sets with a fixed random seed so results are repeatable.

story.label: Model
story.title: A deliberately small model
body: The model is one embedding layer that learns a vector for each word, one simple RNN layer that reads the tweet in order, and a single sigmoid neuron that outputs the probability of positive.

notes.title: Why an embedding layer?
notes.text: One-hot vectors for 10,000 words would be huge and say nothing about similarity. An embedding learns a small vector (32 numbers) per word, and similar words end up with similar vectors.

notes.title: Why a RNN?
notes.text: The meaning of a tweet depends on word order, such as not good versus good, and a recurrent layer reads the words in sequence while carrying a memory.

notes.title: Why return only the last output?
notes.text: I only need one decision per tweet, so the layer passes on its final state rather than an output for every word.

notes.title: Why sigmoid and binary cross-entropy?
notes.text: There are two classes. Sigmoid gives a probability between 0 and 1, and binary cross-entropy is the matching loss.

story.label: Results
story.title: 85.3% accuracy and what it hides
body: It trained for five epochs with a batch size of 64 and scored 85.3% (loss 0.348) on unseen tweets. The confusion matrix showed a bias toward predicting negative, because the data I could download was imbalanced. Balancing by throwing away data would have cost more accuracy than it fixed. A natural improvement is an LSTM, which copes better with vanishing gradients, plus a longer vocabulary and sequence length so long tweets do not lose words.

story.label: Using it

projects.title: Applied Robotics: Q-Learning Taxi
projects.summary: A Q-learning agent that learns to pick up and drop off a passenger on a 5x5 taxi grid, plus a neural network trained to copy the learned policy.
features: Q-learning with learning rate 0.6, discount 0.8 and decaying exploration
Reward design: -1 per step, -10 for a wrong pick-up or drop-off, +20 for a correct drop-off
Learning curve showing rewards rise steeply then stabilise after about 250 episodes
Test functions that run the policy on 1000 random environments
Neural network (MLP classifier) trained on the optimal actions, with loss curve and confusion matrix
projects.whatILearned:
Reward design is the lever. A small penalty on every step pushes the taxi to find the shortest route, a heavy penalty on wrong pick-ups and drop-offs stops it doing those at random, and a bonus for the correct drop-off gives it something to aim for.

Exploration is handled with epsilon: high at the start so the taxi maps out the grid, then decaying to a minimum so it increasingly uses what it learned. The learning curve rises quickly and levels off after about 250 episodes, which shows the policy has settled. I then tested it on 1000 random starting environments to check the average reward was consistent.

In part two I used the Q-table to build a dataset of 400 valid states with their best action and trained a neural network on an 80/20 split. It reached about 67% accuracy, which was only average: the confusion matrix showed it mixing up directions such as north and west. That taught me how much harder it is to imitate a policy than to learn one.

projects.summary: A Java REST API for a health system, built with Jersey (JAX-RS) for a client-server architecture module. It manages doctors, patients, appointments, prescriptions, medical records and billing.
features: Six resources: doctors, patients, appointments, prescriptions, medical records and billing
Create, read, update and delete endpoints for each resource, 32 in total
Endpoints that link records, such as an appointment between a patient and a doctor
Data access layer separate from the resource classes
Custom exceptions mapped to clear HTTP error responses for missing records and invalid input
projects.whatILearned:
The structure is layered: model classes (a shared Person base for doctors and patients), data access classes that hold the data, and resource classes that expose it over HTTP. Keeping those apart meant I could change how data is stored without touching the endpoints.

Error handling was a focus: a not-found exception and a validation exception are each translated by an exception mapper into a proper HTTP response, so clients get a meaningful message instead of a stack trace.

I learned how REST resources are designed around nouns, how path parameters tie related records together, and how to test an API with a client rather than a browser.

story.label: Layers
story.title: Models, data access and resources
body: The structure is layered: model classes (a shared Person base for doctors and patients), data access classes that hold the data, and resource classes that expose it over HTTP. Keeping those apart meant I could change how data is stored without touching the endpoints. There are six resources (doctors, patients, appointments, prescriptions, medical records and billing) with 32 endpoints in total.

story.label: Endpoints
story.title: A resource method, step by step
body: REST resources are designed around nouns, with the HTTP verb saying what to do. Each resource follows the same pattern so that once one makes sense, all of them do.

notes.title: Why path parameters?
notes.text: The id is part of the address, so an appointment lives at a stable URL that a client can store or share.

notes.title: Why produce JSON?
notes.text: The annotation tells the framework to turn the returned object into JSON, so there is no manual formatting.

notes.title: Why throw instead of returning null?
notes.text: A missing record is a normal outcome, but returning null would end as a blank response or a crash. Throwing a named exception lets one handler decide the response.

notes.title: Why log in every method?
notes.text: A line per request makes it possible to see in the server log what the client asked for when something goes wrong.

story.label: Errors
story.title: Errors as proper HTTP responses
body: Error handling was a focus. A not-found exception and a validation exception are each translated by an exception mapper into a proper HTTP response, so clients get a meaningful message and the right status code instead of a stack trace.

notes.title: Why a mapper?
notes.text: The resource methods stay about the happy path and just throw. One mapper per exception type decides the response, so every endpoint reports a missing record the same way.

notes.title: Why status 404?
notes.text: 404 tells the client the thing it asked for does not exist. A plain text message with the id says exactly which record was missing.

notes.title: Why log the error too?
notes.text: The client sees a short message, while the server log keeps the full detail for debugging.

story.label: Data
story.title: Data access and linking records
body: The data access classes hold the records in memory, hand out the next free id, and offer the same set of methods for each resource: get all, get by id, add, update and delete. Related records are linked through the address, such as creating an appointment between a patient and a doctor by putting both ids in the path. Because the API is separate from storage, swapping the in-memory lists for a database would not change any endpoint.

projects.title: R Data Science: Forecasting and Clustering
projects.summary: Two data science tasks in R: forecasting the USD/EUR exchange rate with neural networks, and clustering white wines with k-means, with and without PCA.
features: Forecasting: lagged inputs from the previous days predict the next day's rate
Compared one- and two-hidden-layer networks using RMSE, MAE, MAPE and sMAPE
Clustering: z-score outlier removal, scaling, then k-means
Cluster count checked with four methods: NbClust, elbow, gap statistic and silhouette
PCA keeping components that explain at least 85% of variance (7 components)
Quality checked with silhouette width and the Calinski-Harabasz index
projects.whatILearned:
Forecasting: a time series can be turned into a normal learning problem by giving the network the last few days as inputs. I normalised the data so no input dominated, trained several layouts and scored them with four error measures, because each one hides something the others show. A network with two hidden layers (10 and 8 nodes) beat the best single-layer one, and the predicted-versus-actual plot followed the trend closely with a few outliers.

Clustering: I removed outliers more than three standard deviations from the mean before scaling, since outliers stretch the scale. All four methods agreed that two clusters was the best choice. The clusters overlapped a little, and the average silhouette width was low (about 0.22) on the raw data. After PCA the silhouette score improved, which shows the compressed data separated the wines better.

The main takeaway was to judge a model with several measures and to be honest about what the plots show.

showcase.brief: Side by side to show the improvement.

showcase.alt: R loop that builds a lagged matrix: each row holds five consecutive exchange rates and the next day's rate as the expected value
showcase.caption: Building the lagged inputs for the forecast.

story.label: Forecasting
story.title: Turning a time series into a learning problem
body: The first task forecasts the next day's USD/EUR exchange rate. A time series becomes a normal learning problem by giving the network the last few days as inputs, and I compared three window sizes (five, four and three input days).

notes.title: Why lagged columns?
notes.text: A network predicts one row at a time, so each row needs the history that matters: today and the days before it as inputs, and tomorrow's rate as the answer.

notes.title: Why does the loop start at row 6?
notes.text: The first five days have nothing before them to use, so the first usable row is the sixth. Each shorter window starts one row earlier.

notes.title: Why three window sizes?
notes.text: I did not know how much history helps. Trying five, four and three days showed that the smallest window was enough.

notes.title: Why split by time, not randomly?
notes.text: The first 400 rows train and the remaining rows test, so the model is always tested on days that come after the ones it learned from, like real forecasting.

story.label: Networks
story.title: Comparing networks fairly
body: I normalised the data so no input dominated, trained several layouts and scored them with four error measures (RMSE, MAE, MAPE and sMAPE), because each hides something the others show. A network with two hidden layers (10 and 8 nodes) beat the best single-layer one, and the predicted-versus-actual plot followed the trend closely with a few outliers.

story.label: Clustering
story.title: Clustering wines with k-means
body: For the second task I removed outliers more than three standard deviations from the mean before scaling, since outliers stretch the scale. The number of clusters was checked with four methods (NbClust, elbow, gap statistic and silhouette) and they all agreed that two was the best choice.

story.label: PCA
story.title: Does compressing the data help?
body: PCA kept the 7 components that explain at least 85% of the variance. On the raw data the average silhouette width was low (about 0.22) and the clusters overlapped a little. After PCA the silhouette score improved, which shows the compressed data separated the wines better. The main takeaway was to judge a model with several measures and to be honest about what the plots show.

story.label: Design

body: I drew a use case diagram for what the user can do and a class diagram for how Product, Electronics, Clothing and ShoppingCart relate, and then the code followed it.

story.label: Classes
story.title: Inheritance for the two product types
body: Electronics and Clothing share an ID, name, quantity and price, and each adds its own fields (brand and warranty for electronics, size and colour for clothing). An abstract Product captures what is shared and what every product must be able to do.

notes.title: Why abstract?
notes.text: A generic product never exists on its own, only electronics or clothing. Abstract stops anyone creating one and makes the compiler enforce the contract.

notes.title: Why three abstract methods?
notes.text: Each type prints itself differently, saves a different CSV line and shows different details in the GUI. Abstract methods force every subclass to supply all three.

notes.title: Why call super in the constructor?
notes.text: The shared fields are set once in Product, so Electronics and Clothing only have to deal with their own.

notes.title: Why does getDescription exist?
notes.text: The GUI needs one text line per product. Each subclass builds it from its own fields, so the GUI never has to ask what type a product is.

body: A console menu adds, deletes and lists products (sorted by ID) and saves and loads them from a CSV file. A graphical interface adds a category drop-down and a details panel, and the shopping cart shows the final price with any discount that applies.

story.label: Testing

body: The test plan covered adding, deleting, ordered printing, saving to and loading from the CSV file, opening the GUI and exiting, each with expected results. projects.whatILearned:

projects.title: Cyber Security: Penetration Test Report
projects.summary: A methodology write-up from a penetration testing module, carried out against deliberately vulnerable lab machines that I was authorised to test. It follows the full path from reconnaissance to reporting.
features: Passive reconnaissance: DNS enumeration, public pages and robots.txt
Active scanning: host discovery, SYN and connect scans, UDP scans, service and OS fingerprinting
Web vulnerability analysis: SQL injection, cross-site scripting and command injection in a training app
Password attacks: brute force and dictionary attacks, and recovering hashes
Social engineering and user weakness exercises
Mitigation advice for every finding
projects.whatILearned:
This write-up is about method, not targets: all work was done in an isolated lab, and no real systems, addresses or credentials are shown here.

I learned to work in stages. Passive reconnaissance first, because what you learn from public pages and DNS shapes which scans are worth running. Then active scanning, where the choice of scan matters: a ping sweep and half-open SYN scans are quieter than full connect scans, and I could explain the trade-off between stealth and reliability. Service and OS fingerprinting then turned open ports into specific, checkable findings.

For each weakness (information leaks, injection flaws, weak passwords, trusting users) I paired the attack with the control that prevents it: restricting DNS zone transfers, authentication instead of hiding paths in robots.txt, input validation and parameterised queries, rate limiting and strong password policy. The skill I value most is explaining risk to a non-specialist.

story.title: Input a typo cannot break
body: This was where I first learned that users type the wrong thing, and that a program has to expect it.

notes.title: Why try and except?
notes.text: int() raises an error for anything that is not a whole number. Catching it prints a message and loops again instead of crashing.

notes.title: Why check the allowed range?
notes.text: Only multiples of 20 from 0 to 120 are valid credits, so a number can be an integer and still be wrong.

notes.title: Why while True and break?
notes.text: The loop repeats until the input is acceptable and only then breaks out, which keeps the happy path short.

notes.title: What would I change now?
notes.text: The same loop is copied three times. Today I would move it into one function that takes the prompt as an argument.
